channel_name: The Prof G Show · Scott Galloway
video_title: Why Are We Having Less Sex?
gist: Neuroscientist Debra Soh, author of Sextinction, tells Scott Galloway that one in three American men and one in five women report no sex in the past year, a decline first visible in 2016 data and most pronounced among millennials, Gen Z and young men specifically. The argued mechanism is a stack of substitutes — dating apps with misaligned incentives, ubiquitous and now AI-generated pornography, chatbots and companion products — layered on top of biological factors and a mating market where women's educational and occupational gains concentrate demand on a shrinking pool of high-status men. Galloway frames it as a reversion to the historical norm where roughly 40% of men reproduced, with the post-war middle class as the anomaly.

themes.theme: The measured decline and who it hits

insights.claim: One in three American men and one in five women across all adults, regardless of marital status, report not having had sex in the past year according to the General Social Survey.
insights.speaker: Scott Galloway (citing Sextinction)
insights.so_what: The headline number underpinning every downstream consumer and demographic thesis here — household formation, birth rates, and the entire category of loneliness-adjacent products.

insights.claim: Soh dates the trend to 2016, when nationally representative data first showed millennials as the first generation with a pronounced decline in sexual activity — a pattern that has since been replicated globally and is most acute among Gen Z and young men.
insights.speaker: Debra Soh
insights.so_what: A decade-long, cross-country, replicated trend is a structural demographic input rather than a cultural blip — relevant to any long-horizon model of household formation or fertility.

insights.claim: Soh's frame is that sexual inactivity is a proxy for emotional intimacy and connection more broadly, and that the decline appearing even among married and partnered people is the part that worries her most.
insights.speaker: Debra Soh
insights.so_what: Reframes the metric as a measure of social connection rather than sexual behavior — which makes it a leading indicator for mental health spending, single-person household formation and loneliness-driven consumption.

insights.claim: Roughly half of Gen Z has a diagnosed anxiety disorder with many on medication and antidepressants, and Soh describes the generation as risk-averse in a way that is a symptom of that widespread anxiety.
insights.speaker: Debra Soh
insights.so_what: The mental-health baseline of the cohort is itself a driver of the behavioral changes — and a persistent demand input for mental health services and pharmaceuticals.

insights.claim: A recent poll of 18-30 year olds found more young women hold a negative view of the opposite sex than young men do — only about a third of women under 25 had a positive view of men, versus roughly 70% of men holding a positive view of women.
insights.speaker: Debra Soh
insights.so_what: Cuts against the standard framing that online radicalization runs one way — and a mutual-antipathy equilibrium is a far harder problem to reverse than a one-sided one.

insights.claim: Soh argues dating platforms are structurally misaligned with users: it is not in a dating app's commercial interest for everyone to pair off happily and stop using the product, which is why dating app burnout is now widespread.
insights.speaker: Debra Soh
insights.so_what: The core bear case for dating app businesses: the product either fails users or destroys its own retention, which is now showing up as declining engagement.

insights.claim: Galloway's thesis, which Soh endorses, is that digitizing mating consolidated it the way technology consolidated commerce and search — producing a winner-take-all market where a small number of people have most of the sex and the rest have far less.
insights.speaker: Scott Galloway
insights.so_what: Applies platform-economics logic to a social market — and predicts the same power-law outcomes, which is exactly what the sexual-inactivity data shows.

insights.claim: Soh reports testing AI pornography platforms herself and found them insanely realistic — realistic enough that it scared her — with the user able to simply specify what they want the partner to look like and do.
insights.speaker: Debra Soh
insights.so_what: Personalized generative content removes the last friction in the substitute good — a step change from passive video, and the mechanism by which substitution accelerates from here.
insights.quote: I've tested these platforms out myself and it is insanely realistic. It it scared me how realistic it is.

insights.claim: Soh's neuroscientific mechanism: an orgasm while viewing pornography activates the same brain network as partnered sexual activity, so the reward is delivered without any of the behavior that previously earned it — reinforcing avoidance of the effortful path.
insights.speaker: Debra Soh
insights.so_what: A biological mechanism for behavioral substitution that generalizes beyond sex — the same reward-without-effort structure describes short-form video, gaming and AI companions.

insights.claim: Soh argues sexual frustration historically drove male productivity — building things and demonstrating output because that is what women found attractive — so removing the frustration removes a motivational input.
insights.speaker: Debra Soh
insights.so_what: If the mating incentive that historically drove male labor market effort is being satisfied synthetically, that is a genuine, under-modeled input to male labor force participation.

insights.claim: Soh notes ubiquitous early exposure has made pornography no longer taboo or even interesting to young people — softcore imagery is everywhere in advertising, music videos and entertainment, and young people are seemingly disinterested in it.
insights.speaker: Debra Soh
insights.so_what: Desensitization rather than appetite is the endpoint — which explains why sexualized advertising loses effectiveness with younger cohorts.

insights.claim: Because women outperform their same-age male peers in education and occupation while men do not weight a partner's success heavily, all women effectively compete for the same shrinking pool of successful men — leaving the majority of less successful men shut out of the dating market entirely.
insights.speaker: Debra Soh
insights.so_what: An asymmetric-preferences model that produces market failure from two individually rational behaviors — and explains why the imbalance worsens as women's outcomes improve.

insights.claim: Galloway argues roughly 40% of men and 80% of women have reproduced across history, that the post-war American middle class — GI Bill, highways, seven million returning servicemen made economically viable — was the anomaly, and that rising income inequality is returning society to the historical norm.
insights.speaker: Scott Galloway
insights.so_what: Links mating outcomes directly to income distribution — making the sexual recession a downstream symptom of inequality rather than an independent cultural phenomenon.

insights.claim: Galloway attributes part of the decline to disappearing venues where men can demonstrate value over time — remote work removing the workplace, declining religious attendance, and 40% of UK bars and pubs closing since COVID.
insights.speaker: Scott Galloway
insights.so_what: A physical-infrastructure explanation with commercial implications: the third-place economy that mediated pairing has been structurally destroyed, not merely displaced online.

insights.claim: Galloway argues the majority of young people now don't drink for the first time since tracking began, and that the anti-alcohol movement has a knock-on effect of less inhibition-lowering, less initial contact and therefore less connection — a claim he acknowledges draws pushback.
insights.speaker: Scott Galloway
insights.so_what: Ties the well-documented beverage-alcohol volume decline to the connection decline — a second-order argument that the two consumer trends are causally linked, not coincidental.

insights.claim: Soh points to a biological layer typically excluded from the discussion — the birth control pill's effects on sexual psychology, low testosterone in young men affecting both libido and broader motivation, and environmental toxins — arguing the crisis cannot be fixed without addressing these.
insights.speaker: Debra Soh
insights.so_what: A physiological rather than purely behavioral driver — which if correct points toward testosterone therapy, hormone-alternative contraception and endocrine-disruptor regulation as growth categories.

insights.claim: Soh characterizes reproductive technology — normalized elective single motherhood and egg freezing marketed as buying unlimited time — as band-aid solutions that don't address the root problem, and notes egg freezing is not a sure bet and is messaged as an enabler rather than a last resort.
insights.speaker: Debra Soh
insights.so_what: A skeptical read on the fertility-tech growth story from a researcher: demand is real but built on a success-rate expectation gap that could eventually produce backlash.

insights.claim: Soh describes the 'three sixes' expectation set circulating online — six feet, six figures, and a third physical criterion — noting Galloway's point that excluding married men, obese men and men over 50 leaves roughly 8% of the population meeting it, while defending that both sexes are entitled to their preferences.
insights.speaker: Scott Galloway and Debra Soh
insights.so_what: Quantifies how far online-amplified filtering criteria have moved from the actual distribution — the arithmetic behind the matching failure.

insights.claim: Soh cites a study showing that after 12 weeks of cutting out ultra-processed foods, a third of a depressed sample had their depression remit — offering diet as a high-leverage, low-cost intervention alongside physical activity, sunlight and sleep.
insights.speaker: Debra Soh
insights.so_what: A concrete, quantified nutritional intervention for depression — relevant both as personal advice and as a data point in the food-as-medicine investment thesis.

insights.claim: Soh's advice to women rests on a neuroscience finding: the medial orbitofrontal cortex activates when seeing an attractive face and more strongly when that face is smiling, so visible friendliness is the signal men need to overcome approach anxiety.
insights.speaker: Debra Soh
insights.so_what: A rare mechanistic, testable piece of dating advice grounded in imaging research rather than folk wisdom.

insights.claim: Soh warns that both manosphere and female influencers profit from giving deliberately bad advice — men are told to be dominant and dismissive, women to use men and withhold — because keeping their audience unsuccessful sustains the business.
insights.speaker: Debra Soh
insights.so_what: Identifies the creator-economy incentive that entrenches the antagonism: advice monetization rewards keeping the audience's problem unsolved.

insights.claim: Soh calls for ending diversity initiatives she says explicitly penalize men — citing job postings requiring minority or female status — while Galloway counters that affirmative action should be based on income rather than gender or ethnicity, citing the University of California's post-1997 adversity index.
insights.speaker: Debra Soh and Scott Galloway
insights.so_what: A live policy debate with institutional consequences: class-based versus identity-based preference systems, with UC's adversity index as the working alternative model.

insights.claim: College enrollment is roughly 60/40 female to male, and Soh reports informal affirmative action for men now exists at universities because they are having trouble finding male applicants.
insights.speaker: Scott Galloway and Debra Soh
insights.so_what: Higher education has quietly inverted its own preference regime — a leading indicator of where the male-attainment problem is already being treated as institutional rather than cultural.

insights.claim: Soh says she left academia after publishing an op-ed arguing that childhood gender dysphoria research showed those children were more likely to grow up gay than transgender, knowing it would end her academic career — and describes having had to reverse-engineer study designs toward acceptable findings.
insights.speaker: Debra Soh
insights.so_what: A first-hand account of research-agenda constraint from inside neuroscience — relevant to how much confidence to place in the published literature on contested behavioral questions.

insights.claim: Galloway argues academia's core problem is blocked mobility — the professor who was excellent at GAAP accounting in 1988 won't leave — so talented young researchers now go direct-to-consumer instead, as Soh has.
insights.speaker: Scott Galloway
insights.so_what: Explains the talent drain from universities to independent media as a structural mobility problem rather than an ideological one — with the creator economy as the beneficiary.
